title: Justice, nearest to taqwa
hookLine: a thumb near the scale, and the verse that puts fairness next to mindfulness of Allah

cards: Grapes go on one side of a market scale, a weight on the other, and a thumb hovers just above the pan. Nobody is watching the thumb. That's the whole drama of fairness: much of it happens where no one is checking.
Surah al-Ma'idah gives justice an unexpected neighbor. Not courage. Not law.
In Pickthall's translation: "Deal justly, that is nearer to your duty."

teach.b: Pickthall says duty. In the Arabic of the verse it's taqwa: mindfulness of Allah, guarding yourself, keeping watch over what you do. English struggles to hold it in one word, so translators choose different ones.
And what comes nearest to it? Not a long night of prayer. Not a fast.

The word for justice is 'adl, and its picture is a balance: two sides level, nothing tipped. So taqwa isn't only something on a prayer mat. It shows up at the counter, in how a bill gets split, in how a fight gets retold.

teach.h: THE SKY AND THE SCALE TOGETHER.
teach.b: Second, the sky and the scale. Surah al-Rahman, in paraphrase: He raised the heaven and set up the balance, so do not cheat the balance; keep the weight fair and don't make the measure short. Third, the home.

teach.h: PULPITS OF LIGHT: JUST AT HOME.
teach.b: In Sahih Muslim, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, speaks of people on pulpits of light near Allah.
In paraphrase: those who are just in their judgments, with their families, and in whatever they're put in charge of. The parent dividing the last slice. The older sister picking teams.
The manager handing out the good shifts. And the same verse in al-Ma'idah won't let dislike off the hook: hatred of a people must not push anyone away from justice.
Day six hundred seventy-seven gave that a day of its own. Today's focus is closer: fairness as a way of being mindful of Allah, right where the thumb is.

how: Muslims read al-Ma'idah 5:8 as tying justice to taqwa, and the hadith of the just on pulpits of light extends fairness to judgments, families and anything a person is put in charge of.

o: giving everyone exactly the same, whatever each one needs
punishing wrongdoers as harshly as the law allows
keeping things level and fair, even when nobody's checking

games.q: justice and taqwa — tap the pairs.
p: for the just, even with their families
the sky and the balance together

s: al-Ma'idah calls dealing justly nearer to taqwa
"Deal justly, that is nearer to your duty": Pickthall's word for taqwa is duty.
the hadith of the pulpits of light is only about judges
Muslim: those just in their judgments, with their families, and in what they're put in charge of.
surah al-Rahman mentions the balance right beside the sky
He raised the heaven and set up the balance: so do not cheat the balance.

games.q: you're dividing something good between yourself and a person you don't much like. the verse from al-Ma'idah speaks to this moment. what does it ask?
o: keep the bigger share; you got there first.
deal justly: that is nearer to taqwa.
give it all away so you look generous.
games.why: the verse asks for justice, not a show: deal justly, even when dislike pulls the other way, because that is nearer to taqwa.

practice: Bring to mind something you'll divide or decide today, time, chores, credit for a piece of work, the last of the food, and look at it like a scale: where's your thumb, and is your side quietly a little heavier?
Level that one thing in your mind and see it sitting even. If you pray, you can hold the line from al-Ma'idah: deal justly, that is nearer to your duty.

wordCard.voice: Justice. 'Adl: a balance held level, at the market, at home and in judgment, and called in surah al-Ma'idah nearer to taqwa. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: justice, balance. in 5:8 the command is i'dilu, deal justly.

carryVoice: Your line: nearest to taqwa. Fairness lives right where nobody is checking. Tomorrow, keeping the ties of kin.

sources.q: Deal justly, that is nearer to your duty.
